name: Subharmonic Flechette Launcher SFL-4 'Hornet'
description:
The SFL-4 fires a tight cluster of 24 steel micro-flechettes from a rotating drum magazine, each flechette coated in a piezoelectric polymer that activates on deceleration within soft tissue. The flechettes themselves are not individually lethal — each is 1.8mm in diameter and 12mm long — but the cluster dispersal pattern, combined with the piezoelectric activation sequence that fires as each dart decelerates, creates a cascading internal disruption effect that is grotesquely effective against unarmored targets. Against light armor, the flechettes lack individual penetrating power, but three or four cluster shots against the same panel can compromise soft armor integrity enough to allow subsequent rounds to penetrate.

Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's engineering rationale for the piezoelectric coating was ostensibly medical — the activation signature was derived from research into internal tissue stimulation for nerve damage treatment. The SFL-4 was developed under a security applications contract that repurposed this coating for terminal ballistic enhancement. What distinguishes it from conventional flechette weapons is the sequenced disruption cascade: the flechettes do not all activate simultaneously. The deepest-penetrating darts activate first, creating an internal pressure wave that the shallower darts then amplify, producing a disruption effect far larger than the physical volume of the flechettes would suggest.

The weapon's design is deliberately compact — it resembles an oversized semi-automatic pistol with a wide, cylindrical magazine housing — and it is deceptively light for what it does. Operators describe the firing experience as anticlimactic: a soft pneumatic 'pop' and then the target's reaction to 24 piezo-activated micro-darts is rarely anticlimactic at all. The SFL-4 has a disturbing reputation in field medicine; the flechettes are extremely difficult to locate and remove without specialized scanning equipment.
specifications:
projectile: 1.8mm x 12mm piezoelectric-coated steel micro-flechette
cluster size: 24 flechettes per shot
effective range: 20m (full cluster cohesion) / 35m (partial dispersion)
rate of fire: Semi-automatic, 3-round burst capable
weight: 1.2 kg loaded
magazine capacity: 8 cluster shots per drum (192 flechettes total)
sound signature: Low — pneumatic discharge, sub-70 dB
armor performance: Ineffective against hard plate / degrades soft armor over 3-4 hits
medical complication: Flechettes require dedicated imaging for removal; standard field extraction fails
tactical_use: The SFL-4 is most effective in close-quarters environments against unarmored or lightly armored targets. Operators typically use it as a secondary weapon for unexpected close encounters where a primary long-arm is impractical to bring to bear. In enforcement contexts, it has been used for crowd suppression at close range, though its lethality at standard settings makes 'suppression' a generous characterization. Some operators carry flechette rounds loaded with tracking compounds rather than piezoelectric coating — a modification that allows the weapon to be used for target tagging, though this requires custom drum magazines.
cultural_context: The Hornet is illegal in most jurisdictions not because of its lethality per se but because of the medical complications it creates. Several medical ethics organizations have campaigned against it specifically — the flechette retrieval problem means that wounded targets who survive the immediate hit face serious long-term health consequences even with prompt medical care. This has made it politically toxic, which in turn has made it attractive to certain operators who specifically want to create complications beyond the immediate engagement. Among street operators, it has a nasty reputation as a weapon used by people who want their targets to suffer.
known_users: Street operators seeking deniable close-range capability
Corporate saboteurs targeting personnel rather than infrastructure
story_hooks: A street medic is seeing an unusual number of patients with internal flechette wounds — the imaging signature is unmistakable — but none of the patients will say where they were shot or who did it. They're all from the same district, and they're all frightened. Someone is using a Hornet on civilians and the victims are too scared to talk.

A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric researcher approaches the players claiming the SFL-4's piezoelectric coating was derived from classified medical research that was stolen from her lab. She wants proof of the theft, which would give her legal grounds to challenge Zheng-Dao's patent and potentially shut down production. Zheng-Dao's internal security is already watching her.

A drum magazine of SFL-4 rounds has been recovered from a crime scene, but the flechettes inside are loaded with an unidentified compound instead of the standard piezoelectric coating. Someone is using a Hornet to deliver something — and the players need to determine what before the next shot is fired.
